title: CSS Container Queries
summary: **Container queries** let a component style itself based on the size of its *container* rather than the viewport, enabling truly reusable, context-aware components via `container-type`, `@container`, and container units like `cqi`.

subtopics.title: container-type and container-name
subtopics.explanation: An element becomes a query container when you set container-type. container-type: inline-size lets descendants query its inline (usually width) dimension; size queries both dimensions but requires the container to have a defined size. container-name gives the container a label so a @container rule can target a specific named ancestor. The shorthand container: name / type sets both at once.

subtopics.title: @container queries
subtopics.explanation: @container applies styles to descendants when the nearest matching query container satisfies a size condition, e.g. @container (min-width: 400px) { .card { display: flex; } }. You can target a named container with @container card (min-width: 400px). The condition is evaluated against the container's size, not the viewport — so the same component adapts wherever it's placed.

subtopics.title: Containers vs media queries
subtopics.explanation: Media queries respond to the viewport (or device), which is global; container queries respond to a component's available space, which is local. A card in a wide main column and the same card in a narrow sidebar can look different from each other on the same screen — impossible with media queries alone. Container queries make components self-contained and reusable across layouts.

subtopics.title: Container query units (cqw, cqi, cqh, cqb)
subtopics.explanation: Container units are relative to the query container's size: cqw = 1% of container width, cqh = 1% of container height, cqi = 1% of the inline size, cqb = 1% of the block size, plus cqmin/cqmax. They let you size type and spacing relative to the component's box rather than the viewport — e.g. font-size: clamp(1rem, 5cqi, 2rem) makes text fluid to the container.

subtopics.title: Establishing containment
subtopics.explanation: Setting container-type also establishes layout/style/size containment on the element, which can affect how its own size is computed (notably size containment collapses intrinsic sizing of its contents). inline-size is the common, low-risk choice because it only contains in one axis. Importantly, an element cannot query ITSELF — only descendants can query an ancestor container.

subtopics.title: Common use cases
subtopics.explanation: Reusable cards that switch between stacked and horizontal layouts based on their slot width; widgets dropped into sidebars, modals, or grids that adapt to whatever space they get; design-system components shipped without assumptions about page layout; dashboards where the same chart card behaves correctly in 1-column and 4-column grids.

subtopics.title: Browser support and fallbacks
subtopics.explanation: Container queries are supported in all modern evergreen browsers (Chrome/Edge 105+, Firefox 110+, Safari 16+) as of recent versions. For older browsers, design a sensible default (often the stacked, single-column layout) so the component is usable without the @container enhancement, and optionally use @supports (container-type: inline-size) to scope progressive enhancements.

foundations.overview: Container queries solve a long-standing gap in responsive design: components could only respond to the viewport, not to the actual space they occupy. With container queries, you declare an ancestor as a query container and then style descendants based on that container's size. The result is genuinely portable components — a card knows how to lay itself out whether it lands in a wide hero, a narrow sidebar, or a dense grid.
foundations.formalDefinition: Container queries are a CSS feature that lets descendants of a query container apply styles conditionally on the container's size. An element becomes a container via container-type (inline-size or size); the @container at-rule then matches size conditions against the nearest applicable container, and container units (cqi, cqw, cqh, cqb) express lengths relative to it.
foundations.whyItMatters: They shift responsive design from page-level to component-level, which is how modern design systems and component libraries are actually built and reused. This is a senior-level topic that signals you understand composition, reusability, and the limits of media queries.
foundations.mentalModel: A media query asks 'how big is the window?'. A container query asks 'how big is the box I live in?'. Mark a parent as a container, and its children get to interrogate that parent's size and restyle themselves accordingly — independent of the screen.
foundations.browserPerspective: Declaring container-type establishes containment on the element and registers it as a query container. During layout the browser resolves each container's size, then evaluates @container conditions and container units against the nearest qualifying ancestor for each descendant. Because containers can resize during layout, the engine is careful to avoid infinite layout loops (which is why an element can't size itself from its own container query).
foundations.realWorldUsage: Card components that flip from vertical to horizontal at a width threshold, sidebar widgets, modal/dialog content that adapts to dialog width, dashboard tiles in variable-column grids, and design-system primitives that ship without page-layout assumptions.
foundations.businessImpact: Reusable, context-aware components reduce duplicated CSS and bespoke per-page tweaks, speeding feature delivery and reducing layout regressions across the product.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Components become self-contained and composable: you can drop the same component anywhere and trust it to adapt, which simplifies design systems and reduces coupling between components and page layouts.
foundations.performanceImpact: Establishing containment can actually help the browser optimize layout/paint by limiting recalculation scope. The query evaluation itself is cheap; the main caution is size containment changing intrinsic sizing, which can surprise content-driven layouts.
commonUseCases: Cards that switch stacked vs. horizontal based on slot width
Sidebar/modal widgets that adapt to available space
Design-system components reused across many layouts
Container-relative fluid type with cqi units

commonMisconceptions.myth: An element can query its own size with a container query.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only descendants can query a container; an element can't style itself based on its own container query, which prevents layout feedback loops.
They complement them — media queries are still right for viewport- or device-level concerns (page layout, orientation), while container queries handle component-level adaptation.

commonMisconceptions.myth: container-type: size is the safe default.
commonMisconceptions.reality: size containment requires a defined size and collapses intrinsic sizing; inline-size is the common low-risk choice for width-based queries.

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The wrapper was never declared as a query container, so there's no container for the @container rule to match against and it's ignored. You must set container-type (e.g. inline-size) on the ancestor whose size you want to query.
commonMistakes: Writing @container without setting container-type on an ancestor.
Expecting the queried element itself to be the container (only descendants query an ancestor container).
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Declare the wrapper as an inline-size container so the query has something to match.

debuggingLab.title: Element tries to query itself
debuggingLab.symptom: Setting container-type on .card and querying .card inside @container does nothing.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: A container query only styles DESCENDANTS of the container, never the container element itself — this prevents a feedback loop where restyling the container changes its size and re-triggers the query. The fix is to wrap the content: make an outer element the container and style an inner element.
commonMistakes: Putting container-type on the same element you want to restyle.
Expecting self-querying to work like a media query.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Introduce a wrapper as the container and move the queried styles to the inner element.

theory.question: What are container queries and how do they differ from media queries?
theory.directAnswer: Container queries style a component based on the size of its containing element, whereas media queries respond to the viewport or device. You mark an ancestor with container-type, then use @container size conditions to restyle its descendants. This makes the same component adapt to whatever space it's placed in, so a card can look different in a wide column versus a narrow sidebar on the same screen.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A CSS feature for component-level responsiveness keyed to a container's size rather than the viewport.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Media queries can't express 'respond to my available space', which broke component reuse across different layouts.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: container-type registers a query container; @container matches size conditions against the nearest qualifying ancestor and applies styles to descendants.

theory.whyImportant: It's how modern design systems build genuinely reusable, context-aware components, and it shows an understanding of composition and the limits of viewport-based responsiveness.
theory.realWorldExample: A product card that's stacked in a 4-column grid but becomes horizontal when placed in a wide single-column section — driven by @container, not @media.

nestedTopics.title: container-type
nestedTopics.explanation: inline-size queries width; size queries both axes but needs a defined size.

nestedTopics.title: Descendants only
nestedTopics.explanation: An element can't query itself, only an ancestor container.

nestedTopics.title: Container units
nestedTopics.explanation: cqi/cqw/cqh/cqb size things relative to the container.

followUps.question: When would you still use a media query?
followUps.answer: For viewport- or device-level concerns: overall page layout, orientation, print styles, prefers-color-scheme, and prefers-reduced-motion — things that aren't about a component's local space.

followUps.question: Why can't an element query its own size?
followUps.answer: Restyling the container could change its size, which would re-trigger the query and risk an infinite layout loop; the spec restricts queries to descendants to avoid this.

theory.question: Explain container-type values and container query units.
theory.directAnswer: container-type can be inline-size (query the inline/width axis, the common low-risk choice), size (query both axes, but it applies size containment and needs a defined size), or normal (not a query container, but can still be a style container). Container units are relative to the query container: cqw/cqh are 1% of width/height, cqi/cqb are 1% of the inline/block size, and cqmin/cqmax pick the smaller/larger axis.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The configuration for what an element queries and the length units measured against the container.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To control which dimensions are queryable and to let sizing be relative to the component box rather than the viewport.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: container-type establishes containment and registers the container; container units resolve against that container's resolved size during layout.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing inline-size vs size affects correctness and intrinsic sizing; container units enable component-relative fluid design.
theory.realWorldExample: font-size: clamp(1rem, 5cqi, 2rem) makes a card's heading scale with the card's width regardless of the screen.

nestedTopics.title: inline-size vs size
nestedTopics.explanation: size adds block-axis containment and collapses intrinsic sizing; inline-size is safer for width queries.

nestedTopics.title: cqi vs vw
nestedTopics.explanation: cqi is relative to the container's inline size; vw is relative to the viewport.

nestedTopics.title: container shorthand
nestedTopics.explanation: container: name / type sets container-name and container-type together.

followUps.question: Why is container-type: size riskier than inline-size?
followUps.answer: size applies containment on both axes, which collapses the element's intrinsic block size — content-driven heights can break unless you give it an explicit size.

followUps.question: How do cqmin and cqmax behave?
followUps.answer: cqmin is 1% of the smaller of the container's two axes and cqmax is 1% of the larger, useful for sizing that should respond to the container's shorter or longer side.

scenario.question: You built a card with media queries, but it looks wrong when reused inside a narrow sidebar on a wide desktop screen. How do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: The media query keys off the viewport, which is wide, so the card adopts its wide layout even though its actual slot (the sidebar) is narrow. Convert it to a container query: make the card's wrapper a container with container-type: inline-size and replace @media with @container conditions. The card then adapts to the sidebar's width, not the screen's.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A mismatch between viewport-based responsiveness and a component's local available space.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Media queries are global; a wide viewport doesn't imply a wide slot for the component.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Container queries evaluate the wrapper's resolved size, so the card responds to its real context.

scenario.whyImportant: Reusable components must adapt to where they're placed, not assume the page layout.

nestedTopics.title: Wrap then query
nestedTopics.explanation: Put container-type on a wrapper; style the inner card via @container.

nestedTopics.title: Default-first
nestedTopics.explanation: Keep the stacked layout as the no-query default for resilience.

followUps.question: Would you keep any media queries?
followUps.answer: Possibly for page-level scaffolding (the grid that places the sidebar), while the component itself uses container queries internally.

coding.question: Write CSS for a card that stacks by default and becomes a horizontal media layout when its container is at least 400px wide.
coding.thoughtProcess: Make the wrapper a query container with container-type: inline-size. Default the card to a single-column grid (mobile-first). Add a @container (min-width: 400px) rule that switches the card to a two-column grid for the horizontal layout. Style descendants, never the container itself.
coding.lineByLine: .card-wrap { container-type: inline-size } registers the wrapper as a width-queryable container. .card defaults to a stacked single-column grid with a gap. @container (min-width: 400px) matches the wrapper's inline size; inside it, grid-template-columns: 140px 1fr makes a horizontal thumb + text layout and align-items: center vertically centers them.

alternativeApproaches.title: Named container
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Name the container and target it explicitly for clarity in nested layouts.

alternativeApproaches.title: Media query (limited)
alternativeApproaches.explanation: A @media version works only against the viewport and fails when the card is in a narrow slot on a wide screen.

followUps.question: How would you add container-relative fluid type?
followUps.answer: Use cqi units, e.g. .card h3 { font-size: clamp(1rem, 6cqi, 1.5rem); } so the heading scales with the card's width.

systemDesign.question: Design a responsive strategy for a component library that must work in arbitrary host layouts (grids, sidebars, modals). How do container queries fit, and what are the tradeoffs?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Architect components to be container-query-driven: each component wraps its content in an inline-size query container and styles itself from that container's size, so it adapts to any slot without knowing the host page. Reserve media queries for app-level scaffolding (page grid, orientation, color scheme). Provide a sensible no-query default (usually the stacked layout) for resilience and older browsers, and consider scoping enhancements with @supports.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A component-level responsiveness architecture where adaptation logic lives inside each component via container queries.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A shared library can't assume the consumer's page layout; viewport queries leak global assumptions into reusable components.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each component owns a query container; @container rules and container units drive its internal breakpoints; the host controls only placement and width.

systemDesign.whyImportant: It decouples components from page layout, eliminating per-consumer overrides and reducing layout regressions as the library is reused.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A design-system Card used in a 4-column dashboard grid, a 280px sidebar, and a 700px modal — all rendering correctly because each instance queries its own slot width.

nestedTopics.title: Containers vs media division
nestedTopics.explanation: Components use container queries; the app shell uses media queries.

nestedTopics.title: Containment cost/benefit
nestedTopics.explanation: container-type adds containment that can help paint scoping but can collapse intrinsic sizing with size.

nestedTopics.title: Progressive enhancement
nestedTopics.explanation: Default-first layout plus @supports (container-type: inline-size) for older browsers.

followUps.question: How do you avoid performance issues with many query containers?
followUps.answer: Prefer inline-size (single-axis containment), keep container nesting shallow, and avoid querying deeply nested trees; containment generally helps the browser scope layout/paint work.

followUps.question: How do you document component breakpoints for consumers?
followUps.answer: Publish the container width thresholds (not viewport widths) so integrators know how the component behaves at given slot widths, and expose CSS custom properties for any tunable thresholds.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Container queries push responsiveness into components. A robust architecture splits responsibilities: the application shell uses media queries for page-level layout, orientation, and color scheme, while individual components establish their own query containers and adapt internally. This keeps components portable and the layout system composable.
productionDeepDive.performance: container-type establishes containment, which can help the browser limit layout and paint recalculation scope. Query evaluation is cheap. The main caution is container-type: size, whose two-axis containment collapses intrinsic sizing and can cause layout surprises; inline-size avoids that for width-based queries.
productionDeepDive.security: No direct security surface. As with all layout, contain user-generated content (min/max sizing, overflow handling) so it can't distort a queried component.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Standardize container naming conventions and document component breakpoints as container widths, not viewport widths, so teams integrate components predictably. Expose tunable thresholds via custom properties.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Default-first (stacked) layouts plus @container enhancements degrade gracefully and read clearly. Keep query containers shallow and well-named to avoid ambiguity about which ancestor a @container rule targets.
productionDeepDive.observability: Browser DevTools mark container-query containers and let you inspect which @container conditions currently match; resizing a container in the inspector lets you watch styles flip at thresholds.

caseStudies.company: Component libraries and design systems (broad adoption since 2023)
caseStudies.problem: Components built with media queries broke when reused in narrow slots on wide screens, forcing per-consumer overrides.
caseStudies.solution: Refactored components to own inline-size query containers and adapt via @container, decoupling them from page layout.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Requires a container wrapper per component and careful choice of container-type; older browsers need a sensible default.
caseStudies.lessons: Component-level responsiveness dramatically reduces bespoke overrides and layout regressions across reuse contexts.

keyTakeaways: Container queries style descendants based on a container's size, set via container-type (inline-size or size).
@container matches size conditions against the nearest qualifying container, not the viewport — enabling component-level responsiveness.
An element can only query an ancestor container, never itself, which prevents layout feedback loops.
Container units (cqw/cqi/cqh/cqb) size things relative to the container; cqi enables container-relative fluid type.
Use container queries for reusable components and media queries for viewport/device-level concerns; supported in all modern browsers with a default-first fallback.
